log.entry: Commission accepted: Ground & Velvet — coffee roastery in Ashford

Ground & Velvet: Survey what people hate — the review corpus scan — Scanned 31 documented complaint themes in the review corpus. For a coffee roastery the primary pains are the 28 universal ones (blocking popups, autoplay, dead links, contact hunts, fluff copy, tracking walls, broken mobile, sameness…) plus the commerce pains that bite this niche hardest: hidden-prices, shipping-surprise, detail-missing. Total in scope for this build: 31 pains. Every one becomes a demand, every demand becomes rules on the tasks it feeds.
Ground & Velvet: Convert the findings into build demands — 31 demands locked. Each is injected as a hard rule into the tasks it feeds (26 task kinds governed).

Ground & Velvet: Reason about D1 — OS, input, context — D1 (iOS / Android phones ≤ 640px). Input: touch only — 44px minimum targets, thumb-reach CTA bar. Context: on-the-go, one thumb, interruptions likely. Colour law: high contrast ink on bg; accent reserved for the action bar and key numerals. D1 gets its own arrangement from the book — the coffee roastery reads differently here..

Ground & Velvet: Reason about D2 — OS, input, context — D2 (iPadOS / Android tablets 641–1024px). Input: touch + optional keyboard — hover states must be optional. Context: leaning back, longer sessions, comparison reading. Colour law: surface cards on bgAlt bands; accent2 for secondary highlights. Layout must re-arrange structurally on D2, never just shrink..

Ground & Velvet: Reason about D3 — OS, input, context — D3 (Windows / macOS / ChromeOS laptops 1025–1440px). Input: pointer + keyboard — hover affordances expected. Context: task mode: comparing, shortlisting, filling forms. Colour law: full palette unlocked; ink-panel heroes carry accent numerals. Layout must re-arrange structurally on D3, never just shrink..

Ground & Velvet: Reason about D4 — OS, input, context — D4 (Windows / macOS desktops 1441–1920px). Input: precise pointer, large canvas — density is welcome. Context: deep work, multi-tab comparison. Colour law: bento/tinted cards in surface + accent washes; mega footer on bgAlt. D4 gets its own arrangement from the book — the coffee roastery reads differently here..

Ground & Velvet: Reason about D5 — OS, input, context — D5 (Large displays / TV ≥ 1921px). Input: 10-foot or seated-far viewing — type must scale monumentally. Context: ambient, cinematic, first-impression. Colour law: monumental type on ink or accent2 washes; bgAlt bands alternate. D5 gets its own arrangement from the book — the coffee roastery reads differently here..

Ground & Velvet: Reason about colour — what works where — Global colour law locked: hero washes, card tints and CTA styles are chosen per page from RECIPE_POOL — every recipe must clear its WCAG target before it is allowed. The palette (Harbor Quarry, analogous) provides the roles; dark-mode tokens re-derive and re-check.

findings.hate: Pop-ups and interstitials slamming over the page before anything can be read
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — popup/interstitial usability (Nielsen 2004, reconfirmed 2017); Google interstitial penalty (2017)
findings.demand: Nothing blocks the page. Any notice is inline, small and dismissible.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Audio or video that starts playing uninvited
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — most-hated advertising techniques (Nielsen 2004)
findings.demand: Media stays silent until clicked.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Hero carousels nobody clicks — visitors only ever see slide one
findings.source: Erik Runyon, Carousel Interaction Stats (Notre Dame Web Team, 2013): ~1% engage, 84% see only the first slide
findings.demand: One honest hero; content in static, scannable grids.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Pages that take forever — people give up and never come back
findings.source: Google DoubleClick mobile speed study (2016): 53% of mobile visits abandon past 3 seconds
findings.demand: A fast page: light HTML, lazy images, no junk scripts.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Generic stock-photo smiles that scream "nobody actually works here"
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — Photos as Web Content (Levin 2011): filler photos erode trust
findings.demand: Real, specific imagery with alt text that says what is actually shown.
findings.bite: a coffee roastery sells craft — filler photos would undo the whole story

findings.hate: Being forced to register an account just to look or ask
findings.source: Baymard Institute: roughly one in four abandons when forced to create an account first
findings.demand: Everything works as a guest; accounts optional and honestly labelled.
findings.bite: nobody registers to browse a coffee roastery

findings.hate: Digging through pages to find one working phone number
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — Contact Us usability: users fail when contact facts are buried
findings.demand: Contact everywhere it is needed: nav, footer, its own page, and a full directory.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: No idea who is behind the site — no names, no address, no history
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — "About Us" usability studies (2006, 2016): users seek the humans
findings.demand: Named people, a real address, a since-year, a promise.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Squinting at 12px body text
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — 16px+ body-size guidance for aging eyes
findings.demand: Comfortable, fluid text that never shrinks below readable.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Grey-on-grey text nobody can read
findings.source: WCAG 2.1 contrast minimums (W3C)
findings.demand: Measured contrast, not vibes.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Clicking a link and getting a PDF instead of a page
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — PDF: Still Unfit for Web Reading (Nielsen 2001, reconfirmed)
findings.demand: Information as real web pages.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Clicking something and landing on an error
findings.source: Nielsen — the original web usability heuristics: broken links destroy credibility
findings.demand: Every link lands somewhere real; a 404 that helps when they do not.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Marketing fog — "best-in-class world-class synergy"
findings.source: Morkes & Nielsen, How Users Read on the Web (1997): users scan; fluff is skipped
findings.demand: Plain words, concrete nouns, real numbers.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Fake countdowns, fake scarcity, unsubscribe mazes
findings.source: Brignull — Deceptive Design registry (darkpatterns.org, 2010)
findings.demand: Honest counts, easy outs, no nagging.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Another cookie banner to wrestle before reading one sentence
findings.source: EU consent-fatigue reporting + EDPB guidance on deceptive consent flows
findings.demand: No banner because no tracking.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Proving humanity nine times to send one message
findings.source: Recurring public complaint theme around CAPTCHA gates (widely reported UX rage)
findings.demand: A form that just sends.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Pinch-zooming a site that pretends phones do not exist
findings.source: Google mobile UX guidance: 44px tap targets, viewport sanity
findings.demand: Thumb-sized targets, honest breakpoints, no horizontal scroll.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: A bottomless feed — never finding the thing twice
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — Infinite Scrolling Is Not for Every Website (2013)
findings.demand: Finite, findable grids with an end.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: The menu rearranging itself on every page
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — navigation consistency heuristics
findings.demand: The same nav, same spot, every page.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: A big site with no way to search it
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — site search usability: search is the lifeline on content-heavy sites
findings.demand: A search that actually finds things.
findings.bite: the catalog and journal make this site big enough to need search

findings.hate: Sites that screen readers and keyboards cannot use
findings.source: WHO disability statistics (1.3 billion people); WCAG 2.1
findings.demand: Alt text, landmarks, visible focus, reduced-motion respect.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Forms demanding a life story to ask one question
findings.source: Recurring form-usability finding (NN/g form design usability)
findings.demand: Three fields: name, email, message. Done.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Every template site looks identical — the hero, the cards, the footer, all the same
findings.source: The recurring public complaint "all websites look the same" (long-running theme in web/UX discourse, e.g. template-sameness threads on Hacker News and The Verge)
findings.demand: A site that was arranged, not assembled from the first template on the shelf.
findings.bite: a coffee roastery site that looks like every template loses the trust it needs

findings.hate: Sharing a link and the preview card is broken or empty
findings.source: Open Graph protocol spec (Facebook/Meta) + universal share-card complaints
findings.demand: A real preview image and honest title/description.
findings.bite: the coffee roastery spreads by sharing — broken cards kill the share

findings.hate: Galleries of grey placeholder boxes
findings.source: Recurring marketplace/portfolio review complaint: shipped sites with empty media
findings.demand: Every image slot filled with real bytes before the site ships.
findings.bite: visual proof is the coffee roastery's best argument

findings.hate: Legal pages written to be unreadable
findings.source: Plain-language movement (e.g. US PLAIN Act principles applied to web policies)
findings.demand: Privacy and terms a human can read in one minute.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: A 2019 copyright in the footer — instantly reads as abandoned
findings.source: Recurring credibility-review theme: stale dates signal neglect
findings.demand: A live year in the footer, refreshed on every render — the site reads alive, not abandoned.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Testimonials that read like they were written by the owner at 2am
findings.source: FTC endorsement guides + recurring trust-review complaints about fake-sounding reviews
findings.demand: Voices with names, places and dates — or none at all.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Hunting for a price that is nowhere on the site
findings.source: Baymard Institute checkout research (annual): surprise costs are a leading abandonment cause
findings.demand: Prices plain on the listing AND the detail view.
findings.bite: a coffee roastery visitor decides on price — hide it and they leave

findings.hate: Getting to the last step and discovering extra fees
findings.source: Baymard Institute: extra costs are the top checkout-abandonment cause (annual study)
findings.demand: Every fee named up front — the price on the page is the price you pay.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Product pages with three words and a photo — no specs, no sizes, no proof
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — e-commerce product page usability: users decide on details, not vibes
findings.demand: A detail page that answers the questions before they are asked.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

brief.audience: coffee roastery regulars who notice details
brief.promise: Small-batch, roasted slow. Ground & Velvet keeps that promise in Ashford.
brief.cityStory: We buy green coffee direct from farms we can name — and we do it in Ashford.

D1.why: Banner Ribbon — A tinted ribbon states the seasonal hook above the nav; content flows beneath it. (source: Announcement banner convention (e-commerce UX))

D2.why: Photo Grid 3 — Headline sits above a 3-col photo grid that peeks from the fold; captions on tap. (source: Image-first hero peek (portfolio convention))

D3.why: Double Hero — A slim announcement band (event, seasonal) sits above the main split hero. (source: Announcement hero stacked on main hero)

D4.why: Folio — Story becomes a magazine spread: 7/5 asymmetric columns, drop cap, accent pull-quote spanning the narrow field. (source: Müller-Brockmann asymmetric fields; MDN magazine grid (spans across rows))

D5.why: Cinematic 2200 — Full-bleed ambient stage; monumental centered type (clamp 5.2rem); 5-col features. (source: v2 D5 canonical: ambient stage + monumental type)

Review law [about-trust]: Named people, a real address, a since-year, a promise.
Review law [tiny-type]: Comfortable, fluid text that never shrinks below readable.
Review law [pdf-hate]: Information as real web pages.
Review law [dead-links]: Every link lands somewhere real; a 404 that helps when they do not.
Review law [dark-patterns]: Honest counts, easy outs, no nagging.
Review law [cookie-fatigue]: No banner because no tracking.
Review law [captcha-rage]: A form that just sends.
Review law [mobile-broken]: Thumb-sized targets, honest breakpoints, no horizontal scroll.
Review law [infinite-scroll]: Finite, findable grids with an end.
Review law [nav-drift]: The same nav, same spot, every page.
Review law [a11y-neglect]: Alt text, landmarks, visible focus, reduced-motion respect.
Review law [form-fatigue]: Three fields: name, email, message. Done.
Review law [og-lies]: A real preview image and honest title/description.
Review law [legal-wall]: Privacy and terms a human can read in one minute.
Review law [stale-copyright]: A live year in the footer, refreshed on every render — the site reads alive, not abandoned.
Review law [review-farming]: Voices with names, places and dates — or none at all.
Review law [hidden-prices]: Prices plain on the listing AND the detail view.
Review law [shipping-surprise]: Every fee named up front — the price on the page is the price you pay.

Review law [about-trust]: Named people, a real address, a since-year, a promise.
Review law [tiny-type]: Comfortable, fluid text that never shrinks below readable.
Review law [pdf-hate]: Information as real web pages.
Review law [dead-links]: Every link lands somewhere real; a 404 that helps when they do not.
Review law [dark-patterns]: Honest counts, easy outs, no nagging.
Review law [cookie-fatigue]: No banner because no tracking.
Review law [captcha-rage]: A form that just sends.
Review law [mobile-broken]: Thumb-sized targets, honest breakpoints, no horizontal scroll.
Review law [infinite-scroll]: Finite, findable grids with an end.
Review law [nav-drift]: The same nav, same spot, every page.
Review law [a11y-neglect]: Alt text, landmarks, visible focus, reduced-motion respect.
Review law [form-fatigue]: Three fields: name, email, message. Done.
Review law [og-lies]: A real preview image and honest title/description.
Review law [legal-wall]: Privacy and terms a human can read in one minute.
Review law [stale-copyright]: A live year in the footer, refreshed on every render — the site reads alive, not abandoned.
Review law [review-farming]: Voices with names, places and dates — or none at all.
Review law [hidden-prices]: Prices plain on the listing AND the detail view.
Review law [shipping-surprise]: Every fee named up front — the price on the page is the price you pay.

IronBlue: Survey what people hate — the review corpus scan — Scanned 31 documented complaint themes in the review corpus. For a jazz bar the primary pains are the 28 universal ones (blocking popups, autoplay, dead links, contact hunts, fluff copy, tracking walls, broken mobile, sameness…) plus the commerce pains that bite this niche hardest: hidden-prices, shipping-surprise, detail-missing. Total in scope for this build: 31 pains. Every one becomes a demand, every demand becomes rules on the tasks it feeds.
IronBlue: Convert the findings into build demands — 31 demands locked. Each is injected as a hard rule into the tasks it feeds (26 task kinds governed).

IronBlue: Reason about D1 — OS, input, context — D1 (iOS / Android phones ≤ 640px). Input: touch only — 44px minimum targets, thumb-reach CTA bar. Context: on-the-go, one thumb, interruptions likely. Colour law: high contrast ink on bg; accent reserved for the action bar and key numerals. Layout must re-arrange structurally on D1, never just shrink..

IronBlue: Reason about D2 — OS, input, context — D2 (iPadOS / Android tablets 641–1024px). Input: touch + optional keyboard — hover states must be optional. Context: leaning back, longer sessions, comparison reading. Colour law: surface cards on bgAlt bands; accent2 for secondary highlights. Layout must re-arrange structurally on D2, never just shrink..

IronBlue: Reason about D3 — OS, input, context — D3 (Windows / macOS / ChromeOS laptops 1025–1440px). Input: pointer + keyboard — hover affordances expected. Context: task mode: comparing, shortlisting, filling forms. Colour law: full palette unlocked; ink-panel heroes carry accent numerals. D3 gets its own arrangement from the book — the jazz bar reads differently here..

IronBlue: Reason about D4 — OS, input, context — D4 (Windows / macOS desktops 1441–1920px). Input: precise pointer, large canvas — density is welcome. Context: deep work, multi-tab comparison. Colour law: bento/tinted cards in surface + accent washes; mega footer on bgAlt. D4 gets its own arrangement from the book — the jazz bar reads differently here..

IronBlue: Reason about D5 — OS, input, context — D5 (Large displays / TV ≥ 1921px). Input: 10-foot or seated-far viewing — type must scale monumentally. Context: ambient, cinematic, first-impression. findings.hate: Pop-ups and interstitials slamming over the page before anything can be read
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — popup/interstitial usability (Nielsen 2004, reconfirmed 2017); Google interstitial penalty (2017)
findings.demand: Nothing blocks the page. Any notice is inline, small and dismissible.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Audio or video that starts playing uninvited
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — most-hated advertising techniques (Nielsen 2004)
findings.demand: Media stays silent until clicked.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Hero carousels nobody clicks — visitors only ever see slide one
findings.source: Erik Runyon, Carousel Interaction Stats (Notre Dame Web Team, 2013): ~1% engage, 84% see only the first slide
findings.demand: One honest hero; content in static, scannable grids.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Pages that take forever — people give up and never come back
findings.source: Google DoubleClick mobile speed study (2016): 53% of mobile visits abandon past 3 seconds
findings.demand: A fast page: light HTML, lazy images, no junk scripts.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Generic stock-photo smiles that scream "nobody actually works here"
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — Photos as Web Content (Levin 2011): filler photos erode trust
findings.demand: Real, specific imagery with alt text that says what is actually shown.
findings.bite: a jazz bar sells craft — filler photos would undo the whole story

findings.hate: Being forced to register an account just to look or ask
findings.source: Baymard Institute: roughly one in four abandons when forced to create an account first
findings.demand: Everything works as a guest; accounts optional and honestly labelled.
findings.bite: nobody registers to browse a jazz bar

findings.hate: Digging through pages to find one working phone number
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — Contact Us usability: users fail when contact facts are buried
findings.demand: Contact everywhere it is needed: nav, footer, its own page, and a full directory.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: No idea who is behind the site — no names, no address, no history
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — "About Us" usability studies (2006, 2016): users seek the humans
findings.demand: Named people, a real address, a since-year, a promise.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Squinting at 12px body text
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — 16px+ body-size guidance for aging eyes
findings.demand: Comfortable, fluid text that never shrinks below readable.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Grey-on-grey text nobody can read
findings.source: WCAG 2.1 contrast minimums (W3C)
findings.demand: Measured contrast, not vibes.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Clicking a link and getting a PDF instead of a page
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — PDF: Still Unfit for Web Reading (Nielsen 2001, reconfirmed)
findings.demand: Information as real web pages.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Clicking something and landing on an error
findings.source: Nielsen — the original web usability heuristics: broken links destroy credibility
findings.demand: Every link lands somewhere real; a 404 that helps when they do not.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Marketing fog — "best-in-class world-class synergy"
findings.source: Morkes & Nielsen, How Users Read on the Web (1997): users scan; fluff is skipped
findings.demand: Plain words, concrete nouns, real numbers.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Fake countdowns, fake scarcity, unsubscribe mazes
findings.source: Brignull — Deceptive Design registry (darkpatterns.org, 2010)
findings.demand: Honest counts, easy outs, no nagging.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Another cookie banner to wrestle before reading one sentence
findings.source: EU consent-fatigue reporting + EDPB guidance on deceptive consent flows
findings.demand: No banner because no tracking.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Proving humanity nine times to send one message
findings.source: Recurring public complaint theme around CAPTCHA gates (widely reported UX rage)
findings.demand: A form that just sends.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Pinch-zooming a site that pretends phones do not exist
findings.source: Google mobile UX guidance: 44px tap targets, viewport sanity
findings.demand: Thumb-sized targets, honest breakpoints, no horizontal scroll.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: A bottomless feed — never finding the thing twice
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — Infinite Scrolling Is Not for Every Website (2013)
findings.demand: Finite, findable grids with an end.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: The menu rearranging itself on every page
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — navigation consistency heuristics
findings.demand: The same nav, same spot, every page.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: A big site with no way to search it
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — site search usability: search is the lifeline on content-heavy sites
findings.demand: A search that actually finds things.
findings.bite: the catalog and journal make this site big enough to need search

findings.hate: Sites that screen readers and keyboards cannot use
findings.source: WHO disability statistics (1.3 billion people); WCAG 2.1
findings.demand: Alt text, landmarks, visible focus, reduced-motion respect.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Forms demanding a life story to ask one question
findings.source: Recurring form-usability finding (NN/g form design usability)
findings.demand: Three fields: name, email, message. Done.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Every template site looks identical — the hero, the cards, the footer, all the same
findings.source: The recurring public complaint "all websites look the same" (long-running theme in web/UX discourse, e.g. template-sameness threads on Hacker News and The Verge)
findings.demand: A site that was arranged, not assembled from the first template on the shelf.
findings.bite: a jazz bar site that looks like every template loses the trust it needs

findings.hate: Sharing a link and the preview card is broken or empty
findings.source: Open Graph protocol spec (Facebook/Meta) + universal share-card complaints
findings.demand: A real preview image and honest title/description.
findings.bite: the jazz bar spreads by sharing — broken cards kill the share

findings.hate: Galleries of grey placeholder boxes
findings.source: Recurring marketplace/portfolio review complaint: shipped sites with empty media
findings.demand: Every image slot filled with real bytes before the site ships.
findings.bite: visual proof is the jazz bar's best argument

findings.hate: Legal pages written to be unreadable
findings.source: Plain-language movement (e.g. US PLAIN Act principles applied to web policies)
findings.demand: Privacy and terms a human can read in one minute.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: A 2019 copyright in the footer — instantly reads as abandoned
findings.source: Recurring credibility-review theme: stale dates signal neglect
findings.demand: A live year in the footer, refreshed on every render — the site reads alive, not abandoned.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Testimonials that read like they were written by the owner at 2am
findings.source: FTC endorsement guides + recurring trust-review complaints about fake-sounding reviews
findings.demand: Voices with names, places and dates — or none at all.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Hunting for a price that is nowhere on the site
findings.source: Baymard Institute checkout research (annual): surprise costs are a leading abandonment cause
findings.demand: Prices plain on the listing AND the detail view.
findings.bite: a jazz bar visitor decides on price — hide it and they leave

findings.hate: Getting to the last step and discovering extra fees
findings.source: Baymard Institute: extra costs are the top checkout-abandonment cause (annual study)
findings.demand: Every fee named up front — the price on the page is the price you pay.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Product pages with three words and a photo — no specs, no sizes, no proof
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — e-commerce product page usability: users decide on details, not vibes
findings.demand: A detail page that answers the questions before they are asked.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

tasks.title: Reason about colour — what works where

rules: One thought per element — never blend two ideas into one block.
Concrete nouns beat adjectives; a numeral or proper noun must appear where possible.
Banned words: best, world-class, amazing, unbeatable, #1.
The city and the niche vocabulary must appear naturally.
Recipes are checked against measured contrast, never eyeballed.
A selection of colours is allowed per layout — complementary, never clashing.

tasks.title: Lock the brief — audience, tone, promise
tasks.why: Compress the commission into one audience, one tone, one promise — consistent with the findings.
rules: One thought per element — never blend two ideas into one block.
Concrete nouns beat adjectives; a numeral or proper noun must appear where possible.
Banned words: best, world-class, amazing, unbeatable, #1.
The city and the niche vocabulary must appear naturally.
Audience is one specific group, not "everyone".
Tone from: warm and exact / quietly confident / plain-spoken craft / considered and calm.
The promise must mention the city naturally.
knowledge: Robin Williams, The Non-Designer’s Design Book (1994) — Contrast, Repetition, Alignment, Proximity
Jesse James Garrett, The Elements of User Experience (2002) — audience before pixels

tasks.title: Lock the palette — harmony math + WCAG
tasks.why: Freeze the colour system after every role passes its contrast target.
rules: One thought per element — never blend two ideas into one block.
Concrete nouns beat adjectives; a numeral or proper noun must appear where possible.
Banned words: best, world-class, amazing, unbeatable, #1.
The city and the niche vocabulary must appear naturally.
Harmony math first; correction second.
Every role must pass: ink≥7:1, soft≥4.5:1, accent≥3:1, onAccent≥4.5:1.
knowledge: Josef Albers, Interaction of Color (1963) — colour relationships before colour choice
WCAG 2.1 contrast mathematics

Review law [captcha-rage]: A form that just sends.

Review law [infinite-scroll]: Finite, findable grids with an end.

log.entry: Commission accepted: The Paper Meadow — florist studio in Riverton

The Paper Meadow: Survey what people hate — the review corpus scan — Scanned 31 documented complaint themes in the review corpus. For a florist studio the primary pains are the 28 universal ones (blocking popups, autoplay, dead links, contact hunts, fluff copy, tracking walls, broken mobile, sameness…) plus the commerce pains that bite this niche hardest: hidden-prices, shipping-surprise, detail-missing. Total in scope for this build: 31 pains. Every one becomes a demand, every demand becomes rules on the tasks it feeds.
The Paper Meadow: Convert the findings into build demands — 31 demands locked. Each is injected as a hard rule into the tasks it feeds (26 task kinds governed).

The Paper Meadow: Reason about D1 — OS, input, context — D1 (iOS / Android phones ≤ 640px). Input: touch only — 44px minimum targets, thumb-reach CTA bar. Context: on-the-go, one thumb, interruptions likely. Colour law: high contrast ink on bg; accent reserved for the action bar and key numerals. D1 gets its own arrangement from the book — the florist studio reads differently here..

The Paper Meadow: Reason about D2 — OS, input, context — D2 (iPadOS / Android tablets 641–1024px). Input: touch + optional keyboard — hover states must be optional. Context: leaning back, longer sessions, comparison reading. Colour law: surface cards on bgAlt bands; accent2 for secondary highlights. Layout must re-arrange structurally on D2, never just shrink..

The Paper Meadow: Reason about D3 — OS, input, context — D3 (Windows / macOS / ChromeOS laptops 1025–1440px). Input: pointer + keyboard — hover affordances expected. Context: task mode: comparing, shortlisting, filling forms. Colour law: full palette unlocked; ink-panel heroes carry accent numerals. Layout must re-arrange structurally on D3, never just shrink..

The Paper Meadow: Reason about D4 — OS, input, context — D4 (Windows / macOS desktops 1441–1920px). Input: precise pointer, large canvas — density is welcome. Context: deep work, multi-tab comparison. Colour law: bento/tinted cards in surface + accent washes; mega footer on bgAlt. Layout must re-arrange structurally on D4, never just shrink..

The Paper Meadow: Reason about D5 — OS, input, context — D5 (Large displays / TV ≥ 1921px). Input: 10-foot or seated-far viewing — type must scale monumentally. Context: ambient, cinematic, first-impression. Colour law: monumental type on ink or accent2 washes; bgAlt bands alternate. D5 gets its own arrangement from the book — the florist studio reads differently here..

findings.hate: Pop-ups and interstitials slamming over the page before anything can be read
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — popup/interstitial usability (Nielsen 2004, reconfirmed 2017); Google interstitial penalty (2017)
findings.demand: Nothing blocks the page. Any notice is inline, small and dismissible.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Audio or video that starts playing uninvited
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — most-hated advertising techniques (Nielsen 2004)
findings.demand: Media stays silent until clicked.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Hero carousels nobody clicks — visitors only ever see slide one
findings.source: Erik Runyon, Carousel Interaction Stats (Notre Dame Web Team, 2013): ~1% engage, 84% see only the first slide
findings.demand: One honest hero; content in static, scannable grids.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Pages that take forever — people give up and never come back
findings.source: Google DoubleClick mobile speed study (2016): 53% of mobile visits abandon past 3 seconds
findings.demand: A fast page: light HTML, lazy images, no junk scripts.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Generic stock-photo smiles that scream "nobody actually works here"
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — Photos as Web Content (Levin 2011): filler photos erode trust
findings.demand: Real, specific imagery with alt text that says what is actually shown.
findings.bite: a florist studio sells craft — filler photos would undo the whole story

findings.hate: Being forced to register an account just to look or ask
findings.source: Baymard Institute: roughly one in four abandons when forced to create an account first
findings.demand: Everything works as a guest; accounts optional and honestly labelled.
findings.bite: nobody registers to browse a florist studio

findings.hate: Digging through pages to find one working phone number
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — Contact Us usability: users fail when contact facts are buried
findings.demand: Contact everywhere it is needed: nav, footer, its own page, and a full directory.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: No idea who is behind the site — no names, no address, no history
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — "About Us" usability studies (2006, 2016): users seek the humans
findings.demand: Named people, a real address, a since-year, a promise.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Squinting at 12px body text
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — 16px+ body-size guidance for aging eyes
findings.demand: Comfortable, fluid text that never shrinks below readable.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Grey-on-grey text nobody can read
findings.source: WCAG 2.1 contrast minimums (W3C)
findings.demand: Measured contrast, not vibes.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Clicking a link and getting a PDF instead of a page
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — PDF: Still Unfit for Web Reading (Nielsen 2001, reconfirmed)
findings.demand: Information as real web pages.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Clicking something and landing on an error
findings.source: Nielsen — the original web usability heuristics: broken links destroy credibility
findings.demand: Every link lands somewhere real; a 404 that helps when they do not.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Marketing fog — "best-in-class world-class synergy"
findings.source: Morkes & Nielsen, How Users Read on the Web (1997): users scan; fluff is skipped
findings.demand: Plain words, concrete nouns, real numbers.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Fake countdowns, fake scarcity, unsubscribe mazes
findings.source: Brignull — Deceptive Design registry (darkpatterns.org, 2010)
findings.demand: Honest counts, easy outs, no nagging.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Another cookie banner to wrestle before reading one sentence
findings.source: EU consent-fatigue reporting + EDPB guidance on deceptive consent flows
findings.demand: No banner because no tracking.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Proving humanity nine times to send one message
findings.source: Recurring public complaint theme around CAPTCHA gates (widely reported UX rage)
findings.demand: A form that just sends.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Pinch-zooming a site that pretends phones do not exist
findings.source: Google mobile UX guidance: 44px tap targets, viewport sanity
findings.demand: Thumb-sized targets, honest breakpoints, no horizontal scroll.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: A bottomless feed — never finding the thing twice
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — Infinite Scrolling Is Not for Every Website (2013)
findings.demand: Finite, findable grids with an end.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: The menu rearranging itself on every page
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — navigation consistency heuristics
findings.demand: The same nav, same spot, every page.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: A big site with no way to search it
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — site search usability: search is the lifeline on content-heavy sites
findings.demand: A search that actually finds things.
findings.bite: the catalog and journal make this site big enough to need search

findings.hate: Sites that screen readers and keyboards cannot use
findings.source: WHO disability statistics (1.3 billion people); WCAG 2.1
findings.demand: Alt text, landmarks, visible focus, reduced-motion respect.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Forms demanding a life story to ask one question
findings.source: Recurring form-usability finding (NN/g form design usability)
findings.demand: Three fields: name, email, message. Done.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Every template site looks identical — the hero, the cards, the footer, all the same
findings.source: The recurring public complaint "all websites look the same" (long-running theme in web/UX discourse, e.g. template-sameness threads on Hacker News and The Verge)
findings.demand: A site that was arranged, not assembled from the first template on the shelf.
findings.bite: a florist studio site that looks like every template loses the trust it needs

findings.hate: Sharing a link and the preview card is broken or empty
findings.source: Open Graph protocol spec (Facebook/Meta) + universal share-card complaints
findings.demand: A real preview image and honest title/description.
findings.bite: the florist studio spreads by sharing — broken cards kill the share

findings.hate: Galleries of grey placeholder boxes
findings.source: Recurring marketplace/portfolio review complaint: shipped sites with empty media
findings.demand: Every image slot filled with real bytes before the site ships.
findings.bite: visual proof is the florist studio's best argument

findings.hate: Legal pages written to be unreadable
findings.source: Plain-language movement (e.g. US PLAIN Act principles applied to web policies)
findings.demand: Privacy and terms a human can read in one minute.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: A 2019 copyright in the footer — instantly reads as abandoned
findings.source: Recurring credibility-review theme: stale dates signal neglect
findings.demand: A live year in the footer, refreshed on every render — the site reads alive, not abandoned.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Testimonials that read like they were written by the owner at 2am
findings.source: FTC endorsement guides + recurring trust-review complaints about fake-sounding reviews
findings.demand: Voices with names, places and dates — or none at all.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Hunting for a price that is nowhere on the site
findings.source: Baymard Institute checkout research (annual): surprise costs are a leading abandonment cause
findings.demand: Prices plain on the listing AND the detail view.
findings.bite: a florist studio visitor decides on price — hide it and they leave

findings.hate: Getting to the last step and discovering extra fees
findings.source: Baymard Institute: extra costs are the top checkout-abandonment cause (annual study)
findings.demand: Every fee named up front — the price on the page is the price you pay.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

findings.hate: Product pages with three words and a photo — no specs, no sizes, no proof
findings.source: Nielsen Norman Group — e-commerce product page usability: users decide on details, not vibes
findings.demand: A detail page that answers the questions before they are asked.
findings.bite: universal pain — every visitor feels it

D1.why: Endless Fold — Five sections, each sized to one phone viewport; scroll feels like turning pages. (source: One-thought-per-screen scroll (poster editorial))

D2.why: Editorial Two — Story runs as 2 magazine fields with a pull-quote spanning the narrow one; drop cap retained. (source: Müller-Brockmann fields at tablet; MDN magazine grid)

D3.why: Aurora — Single center axis. Kicker → H1 → lede → two CTAs stacked down the middle; stats band dark; cards 3-up. (source: Z-pattern for low-density pages (NN/g); Material 12-col responsive grid)

D4.why: Parallel Nav — Nav, breadcrumb and content run as parallel columns; sections numbered. (source: Documentation-style parallel columns)

D5.why: Cathedral — Everything centers on a single ceremonial axis; nav letter-spaced; sections symmetrical. (source: Müller-Brockmann ceremonial centering (poster series))

art.productNotes: Catalog law for 0 products: the catalog must survive the skim test: scannable names, honest prices, tags only when true. Each product earns its own detail page, its own image slot, its own alt text.

tasks.title: Survey what people hate — the review corpus scan
tasks.why: Read the corpus of documented public complaints and user research; select the pains that bite for this niche.
rules: One thought per element — never blend two ideas into one block.
Concrete nouns beat adjectives; a numeral or proper noun must appear where possible.
Banned words: best, world-class, amazing, unbeatable, #1.
The city and the niche vocabulary must appear naturally.
Cite the source of every pain you keep.
Universal pains always stay; commerce pains join when the niche sells.
Every selected pain must carry a demand.
knowledge: The reasoner’s review corpus (COMPLAINT_CORPUS): NN/g, Baymard, Google speed research, WCAG, Deceptive Design registry

rules: One thought per element — never blend two ideas into one block.

D1–D5 media blocks present; the page’s per-device layout overrides stamped.
Nav identical to every other page (consistency law).
Review law [popup-walls]: Nothing blocks the page. Any notice is inline, small and dismissible.
Review law [autoplay-sound]: Media stays silent until clicked.
Review law [carousel-ignore]: One honest hero; content in static, scannable grids.
Review law [speed-death]: A fast page: light HTML, lazy images, no junk scripts.
Review law [forced-accounts]: Everything works as a guest; accounts optional and honestly labelled.
Review law [contact-hunt]: Contact everywhere it is needed: nav, footer, its own page, and a full directory.
Review law [about-trust]: Named people, a real address, a since-year, a promise.
Review law [tiny-type]: Comfortable, fluid text that never shrinks below readable.
Review law [pdf-hate]: Information as real web pages.
Review law [dead-links]: Every link lands somewhere real; a 404 that helps when they do not.
Review law [dark-patterns]: Honest counts, easy outs, no nagging.
Review law [cookie-fatigue]: No banner because no tracking.
Review law [captcha-rage]: A form that just sends.
Review law [mobile-broken]: Thumb-sized targets, honest breakpoints, no horizontal scroll.
Review law [infinite-scroll]: Finite, findable grids with an end.
Review law [nav-drift]: The same nav, same spot, every page.
Review law [a11y-neglect]: Alt text, landmarks, visible focus, reduced-motion respect.
Review law [form-fatigue]: Three fields: name, email, message. Done.
Review law [og-lies]: A real preview image and honest title/description.
Review law [legal-wall]: Privacy and terms a human can read in one minute.
Review law [stale-copyright]: A live year in the footer, refreshed on every render — the site reads alive, not abandoned.
Review law [review-farming]: Voices with names, places and dates — or none at all.
Review law [hidden-prices]: Prices plain on the listing AND the detail view.
Review law [shipping-surprise]: Every fee named up front — the price on the page is the price you pay.
